MemDerive: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Agent Memory over Evolving Data

Sen Gao Affiliation: National University of Singapore, Singapore, Singapore email: sen@u.nus.edu , Yongan Li Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China email: liyongan@sjtu.edu.cn , Han Chen Affiliation: National University of Singapore, Singapore, Singapore email: chenhan@u.nus.edu , Bingsheng He Affiliation: National University of Singapore, Singapore, Singapore email: dcsheb@nus.edu.sg , Ming Wu Affiliation: Zero Gravity Labs, Singapore, Singapore email: ming@0g.ai , Jason Zeng Affiliation: Zero Gravity Labs, Singapore, Singapore email: jason@0g.ai , Michael Heinrich Affiliation: Zero Gravity Labs, Singapore, Singapore email: michael@0g.ai and Shixuan Sun Affiliation: Shanghai Jiao Tong University, Shanghai, China email: sunshixuan@sjtu.edu.cn
Abstract.

Long-running agents rely on memory of their past interactions for task state, such as what has been completed and which conditions still hold. Such state is usually a derived state. No record states it, and it must be computed by rules from multiple records of an evolving history. Existing memory benchmarks score only the final answer, with no reference for the intermediate states behind it. A wrong answer therefore cannot be traced to the state that was missed, and a state that silently became outdated goes undetected. We present MemDerive, a diagnostic benchmark for agent memory over evolving data. It specifies each scenario symbolically, derives exact gold answers with Datalog, records the gold derivation DAG and the supporting events of every query, and renders the history in natural language with fictional entities and distractors. Its 10 scenarios contain 4,692 events and 1,503 queries whose difficulty varies along access, evolution, and composition. On this ground truth, MemDerive evaluates answer reliability, diagnoses failures by probing the nodes of the gold derivation DAG, and tracks whether answers stay correct as events arrive.

Our evaluation of four memory systems reveals failures that final-answer benchmarks hide. On derived state, every memory system falls behind simple BM25 retrieval, although the same answer model reaches 96.01 % when given the supporting events. Most failures are ungathered, as a system holds the missing intermediate state but does not retrieve it for the question that needs it. Memory systems also rarely propagate implicit changes, which no new record states. These results suggest three principles for memory design. Gather inputs along the derivation, store rules with their versions, and maintain derived states through recorded dependencies.

1. Introduction

Long-running agents rely on memory of their past interactions to decide what to do next (Wang et al., 2024b; Sumers et al., 2024). A decision depends on what has been completed, which conditions still hold, and what remains to be done. Anthropic reports coding agents that prematurely consider a project complete and addresses this with persistent progress records and verification across sessions (Young, 2025). Generative agents (Park et al., 2023) and Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023) likewise synthesize past observations into reflections that guide later behavior. In both cases the agent needs a task state that the records of its history support but rarely state. Memory systems such as Mem0 (Chhikara et al., 2025) and Cognee (Markovic et al., 2025) extract information from the history and retrieve what matches a request. This paper asks whether they supply the state that a task needs.

Figure 1 shows the difference on a LoCoMo history. The original question asks which futuristic game Nate reported playing, and one record answers it. Now Nate asks what he could play to relax away from competitive gaming. A good answer lists the games he has played without any recorded tournament. No record states this set. Memory must first build two intermediate states from several sessions, the games Nate has played and the games he played in tournaments, and then take their difference. We call a fact that no record states but that follows from several records by rules a derived state, and a question whose answer is a derived state a state question. The status of a task is a typical derived state. Like the result of a view over database tables, a derived state is computed from the history rather than stored in it. Here, however, the base data is natural language, and the view is defined only when a question arrives.

Derived state is hard for memory systems. The records that support it rarely share words with the question and have low embedding similarity to it. They matter only in combination, and together they can outnumber any retrieval budget. A derived state is usually composed from intermediate states layer by layer, so one wrong intermediate state corrupts every state above it. It can also become stale without any record saying so. A later record that Nate entered a Chess tournament would remove Chess from the answer, although it never mentions the games he could play to relax. These properties affect every way of building memory, whether a system retrieves raw records for each question, extracts and stores facts as events arrive, or searches and reasons over the history when a question arrives.

A paired study shows that current memory systems fail on state questions. We take histories from LoCoMo and LongMemEval, keep an original question, and add a state question over the same history and the same stored memories. Figure 2(a) shows Mem0 falling from 86.7 % to 33.3 % and Cognee from 60.0 % to 16.7 %. Given the whole history, the same answer model still reaches 86.7 %, so the questions are answerable and the loss lies in what memory supplies. Figure 2(b) splits each state question into two sub-questions, one for each intermediate state. Retrieving separately for each sub-question helps some systems, and so does answering the state question from the system’s own answers to the sub-questions, but no system exceeds 46.7 %. Given the correct answers to the sub-questions, the answer model solves every state question. The bottleneck is therefore obtaining the intermediate states, not combining them, and an evaluation that scores only final answers cannot see it.

Existing benchmarks were not designed to expose this failure. LoCoMo and LongMemEval test recall, temporal and multi-session reasoning, and knowledge updates over long conversations (Maharana et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025). StateMemBench separates current from superseded answers (Fan et al., 2026), and MemTrace audits how evidence is reached and used (Long et al., 2026). These benchmarks judge the final answer. Their histories are written text without executable semantics, so they cannot supply the correct value of an intermediate state, and a wrong answer cannot be traced to the step that failed (Table 6). Their updates are explicit, since a new record revises a fact and states its new value. A derived state also changes implicitly, when a fact it depends on changes and no record mentions the state. Rankings on these benchmarks therefore do not carry over to derived state. On LongMemEval, Mem0 reaches 84.00 % and exceeds BM25 at 78.60 %, yet on derived state every memory system falls behind BM25.

Our approach. We present MemDerive, a diagnostic benchmark for agent memory over evolving data. Its design follows from four needs. Exact ground truth. Every intermediate state needs a correct value at every point of an evolving history. MemDerive therefore specifies each scenario symbolically. Each event pairs a natural-language record with symbolic actions, and a Datalog program with aggregation derives every state from the current facts and rules, so the gold is exact by construction. Derivations as evidence. For each query, MemDerive records a gold derivation DAG that links the answer through its intermediate states to the events, and the witnesses, the minimal sets of events that support the answer. No shortcuts. The answer must come from the history alone. No record states a derived state, every recognizable entity is fictional so that pretrained knowledge cannot help, and the key terms of a question often appear only in distractor records. Controlled difficulty. Generation varies three workload dimensions independently, namely Access to the support, Evolution of the facts, and Composition of the derivation, so that a failure can be traced to one of them. The suite covers travel reimbursement, shopping, and degree planning in 10 scenarios with 4,692 events and 1,503 queries.

Memory systems share no interface beyond answering questions, so MemDerive observes them as black boxes through three evaluation questions. Q1: Reliability compares answers exactly with the gold and citations with the witnesses. Q2: Diagnosis turns the nodes of each gold derivation DAG into state probes, questions about single intermediate states. Following the DAG from the answer toward the events, it locates the lowest states that the system gets wrong, classifies why they fail, and tests whether repairing them recovers the answer. Q3: Maintenance asks tracked queries at successive checkpoints and separates the refresh of changed answers from the preservation of unchanged ones.

Findings and implications. We evaluate four memory systems and two raw-retrieval baselines under one answer model. First, memory systems answer 30.41–48.30 % of the queries, below BM25 at 58.28 %, whereas the whole history yields 79.84 % and the supporting events 96.01 %. Accuracy falls along all three workload dimensions, also under matched context budgets. Second, most failures are ungathered. The system answers a missing intermediate state correctly when asked about it directly, but does not retrieve it for the question that needs it. Rebuilding the answer from these intermediate answers recovers up to 30.0 points of accuracy, so a memory system should split a request for a derived state into requests for its inputs. Some systems fail to return rules even when asked directly, so rules should be stored with their versions, like facts. Third, memory systems preserve 91.03–92.86 % of unchanged answers and refresh 82.4 % of explicit changes, which a new record states, but only 41.1 % of implicit changes, which propagate through dependencies. Stored states therefore need recorded dependencies, as in incremental view maintenance (Gupta et al., 1993; Motik et al., 2015). Their work at ingestion buys neither accuracy nor refresh.

Our contributions are as follows.

  • •

    Problem characterization. We define derived state over an evolving history, identify the properties that make it hard for memory systems, and derive three workload dimensions, connecting agent memory to views and provenance (Section 2).

  • •

    Benchmark construction. Executable scenarios generate histories and queries with exact gold derivations, witnesses, and controlled workload dimensions (Section 3).

  • •

    Evaluation methodology. State probes in two contexts locate and classify failures, two recoveries test them, and tracked queries separate refresh from preservation (Section 4).

  • •

    Experimental study. A comprehensive evaluation of four memory systems and two retrieval baselines over a broad set of metrics yields three findings and design lessons for memory systems (Sections 5 and 6).

Reproducibility. The benchmark dataset is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DeriveMem-67C6, and the evaluation framework that runs all experiments is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DerivEval-6799.

2. Derived State over Evolving Data

This section defines derived state over an evolving history and derives its workload dimensions and its implications for memory systems and their evaluation. Table 1 summarizes the notation.

2.1. Data Model

A memory system ingests a history of events.

Definition 0 (Event and history).

An event ee is a triple (te,re,Ae)(t_{e},r_{e},A_{e}) of an observation time tet_{e}, a natural-language record rer_{e}, and a nonempty set AeA_{e} of actions. Each event has a unique identifier. An action asserts a fact or declares a rule. A history OO is a set of events.

A memory system reads only the records rer_{e} and cites events by their identifiers. Gold answers depend only on the actions AeA_{e}.

Versions and cutoff. A fact can be asserted more than once. Each assertion creates a version of the fact, and a revision or cancellation supersedes the previous version, which then becomes obsolete (Snodgrass and Ahn, 1985). Which versions are visible depends on time. Every query fixes an observation cutoff τ\tau, and the events known at that point are O≤τ={e∈O:te≤τ}O_{\leq\tau}=\{e\in O:t_{e}\leq\tau\}.

Definition 0 (Resolved state).

The resolved state Bτ=𝖱𝖾𝗌𝗈𝗅𝗏𝖾⁡(O≤τ)B_{\tau}={\mathsf{Resolve}}(O_{\leq\tau}) contains, for every fact, the latest version visible at τ\tau:

(1) 𝖼𝗎𝗋(f,e)←e∈O≤τ,f∈Ae,¬𝗌𝗎𝗉𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖽𝖾𝖽(f,e,τ).{\mathsf{cur}}(f,e)\leftarrow e\in O_{\leq\tau},\ f\in A_{e},\ \neg\,{\mathsf{superseded}}(f,e,\tau).

Here f∈Aef\in A_{e} means that an action of ee asserts a version of the fact ff, and 𝗌𝗎𝗉𝖾𝗋𝗌𝖾𝖽𝖾𝖽⁡(f,e,τ){\mathsf{superseded}}(f,e,\tau) holds when a later event in O≤τO_{\leq\tau} asserts a newer version of ff. Rules declared by events are versioned and resolved in the same way, so BτB_{\tau} also holds the current version of each rule.

2.2. Derived State and Queries

Definition 0 (Derivation program, closure, derived state).

The derivation program PτP_{\tau} consists of the fixed rules of the domain and the current rules in BτB_{\tau}. It is a Datalog program extended with stratified negation and aggregation (Abiteboul et al., 1995; Apt et al., 1988; Consens and Mendelzon, 1993). The closure Cτ=𝖣𝖾𝗋𝗂𝗏𝖾⁡(Pτ,Bτ)C_{\tau}={\mathsf{Derive}}(P_{\tau},B_{\tau}) is the set of facts that PτP_{\tau} derives from BτB_{\tau}, and a derived state is a fact in Cτ∖BτC_{\tau}\setminus B_{\tau}.

The closure is obtained by applying the rules to the resolved state until a fixpoint is reached. It holds everything the history entails at τ\tau and can be very large, so the benchmark never materializes it and computes only the states that its queries need. Because events declare rules, PτP_{\tau} evolves together with the data.

Example 0 (Rules for Example 2.3).

Three rules derive the target. Each rule derives its left side whenever its right side holds, and 𝖽𝖾𝗌𝗍\mathsf{dest} gives the current booking city of a trip in BτB_{\tau}:

𝖼𝗈𝗎𝗇𝗍𝗋𝗒⁡(T,N)\displaystyle{\mathsf{country}}(T,N) ←𝖽𝖾𝗌𝗍⁡(T,C),𝖼𝗂𝗍𝗒𝖨𝗇⁡(C,N)\displaystyle\leftarrow{\mathsf{dest}}(T,C),\ {\mathsf{cityIn}}(C,N)
𝗁𝗈𝗆𝖾⁡(P,N)\displaystyle{\mathsf{home}}(P,N) ←𝖻𝖺𝗌𝖾𝖽𝖨𝗇⁡(P,C),𝖼𝗂𝗍𝗒𝖨𝗇⁡(C,N)\displaystyle\leftarrow{\mathsf{basedIn}}(P,C),\ {\mathsf{cityIn}}(C,N)
𝗈𝗎𝗍𝗌𝗂𝖽𝖾⁡(P,T)\displaystyle{\mathsf{outside}}(P,T) ←𝗍𝗋𝗂𝗉⁡(P,T),𝖼𝗈𝗎𝗇𝗍𝗋𝗒⁡(T,N),\displaystyle\leftarrow{\mathsf{trip}}(P,T),\ {\mathsf{country}}(T,N),
𝗁𝗈𝗆𝖾⁡(P,M),N≠M.\displaystyle\phantom{\leftarrow{}}\ {\mathsf{home}}(P,M),\ N\neq M.

The query counts the facts 𝗈𝗎𝗍𝗌𝗂𝖽𝖾⁡(Vera,T){\mathsf{outside}}(\text{Vera},T). In August the count is two, for Trip-Anser and Trip-Ibex.

Definition 0 (Query and gold answer).

A query q=(θ,τ)q=(\theta,\tau) is a natural-language question that asks for a derived state θ\theta, called its target, at cutoff τ\tau. Its gold answer z⁡(q)=(ℓq,yq)z(q)=(\ell_{q},y_{q}) consists of an answerability label ℓq\ell_{q} and an answer yqy_{q}, both determined by CτC_{\tau}. The answer can be an entity, a set, a Boolean, or a number.

Answerability. Not every query can be answered from the history. The label ℓq\ell_{q} is 𝖺𝗇𝗌𝗐𝖾𝗋𝖺𝖻𝗅𝖾\mathsf{answerable} when the history determines the answer, 𝗃𝗎𝗌𝗍𝗂𝖿𝗂𝖾𝖽​-​𝗓𝖾𝗋𝗈\mathsf{justified\text{-}zero} when it determines that the answer is zero or empty, and 𝗎𝗇𝗄𝗇𝗈𝗐𝗇\mathsf{unknown} when it does not determine the answer, in which case yq=⊥y_{q}=\bot. For a count, total, or empty set, the history determines the answer only if some event asserts that the collection is complete (Reiter, 1978; Levy, 1996; Razniewski and Nutt, 2011).

2.3. Gold Derivations and Witnesses

An answer alone cannot show which inputs a system used or where it went wrong. MemDerive therefore records, for every query, how its gold answer follows from the history.

Definition 0 (Gold derivation DAG).

The gold derivation DAG 𝒢q\mathcal{G}_{q} of query qq is a finite directed acyclic graph whose root is the target of qq. Its inner nodes are the derived states on which the root depends, called intermediate states, together with the resolved facts and rules used to derive the root. Its leaves are the events that assert these facts and declare these rules. Each edge points from a node to an input it needs, called a child. When the answer is 𝗎𝗇𝗄𝗇𝗈𝗐𝗇\mathsf{unknown}, a leaf marks the missing fact instead of an event.

A shared input can serve several parents, so the structure is a DAG rather than a tree. The height of 𝒢q\mathcal{G}_{q} is the length of its longest path from the root, and its width is the largest number of nodes at the same depth. Height measures how deep a derivation is, and width measures how many inputs it combines at one level. Because every intermediate state is a node with a known gold state, an answer can be checked step by step rather than only at the root.

Definition 0 (Support and witness).

The support S⁡(q)S(q) of query qq is the set of events that contribute to some derivation of z⁡(q)z(q). A witness of qq is a minimal subset W⊆S⁡(q)W\subseteq S(q) from which z⁡(q)z(q) can be derived, and 𝒲⁡(q)\mathcal{W}(q) denotes the set of all witnesses of qq.

A query can have several witnesses, because several events can assert the same fact. The definition of a witness follows minimal why-provenance (Buneman et al., 2001). An event outside S⁡(q)S(q) whose record resembles relevant information is a distractor for qq.

Example 0 (Gold derivation for Example 2.3).

Figure 3 shows 𝒢q\mathcal{G}_{q} at the August cutoff. The only witness is {e1,…,e6,e8,e9,e10}\{e_{1},\ldots,e_{6},e_{8},e_{9},e_{10}\}. It excludes the obsolete e7e_{7} and the distractor e11e_{11} but still contains nine of the eleven events. Every fact in this history is asserted by a single event, so S⁡(q)S(q) equals the only witness. Before e9e_{9} arrives, no event asserts that the trip list is complete, so the label is 𝗎𝗇𝗄𝗇𝗈𝗐𝗇\mathsf{unknown}, although three foreign trips are already visible.

2.4. Characteristics and Workload Dimensions

A recorded fact is stated by one record, rests on that record alone, depends on no other state, and changes only when an event asserts a new version of it. Derived state differs in all four respects.

Property 1 (Implicitness).

No record states a derived state, so it can only be computed from facts by rules. A query uses the vocabulary of derived predicates, whereas records use the vocabulary of recorded facts.

Property 2 (Joint support).

A derived state rests on a set of events that are relevant only together. The set can be large, and the answer needs all of it.

Property 3 (Layered dependence).

A derived state is composed from intermediate states, layer by layer, and the same intermediate state is shared by many queries. If a system derives an intermediate state incorrectly, the error can propagate to every state above it.

Property 4 (Indirect change).

A derived state changes whenever one of its inputs, a fact or a rule, changes, even if no new event mentions it. One event can therefore change many derived states at once.

Example 0 (Characteristics of Example 2.3).

All four characteristics appear in the running example. No record states the count. The full TripOps query behind the example asks about trips abroad, and the only records containing that word are distractors such as e11e_{11}. The Corby booking in e10e_{10} is relevant only together with e5e_{5} and e1e_{1}, which place Vera in Corvia, and the full query has a witness of 44 events. The count is composed from the foreign-trip set, which is composed from the country of each trip, and Vera’s home country is shared by every query about her travel. Finally, e10e_{10} concerns a hotel, yet it changes the count.

Workload dimensions. We call the set of queries that a benchmark asks its workload. Answering a derived-state query requires three steps, which Figure 3 draws as the three layers of the running example. The difficulty of each step can be varied independently, so each step defines one workload dimension of MemDerive. ➊ Access gathers the full support of the answer (Properties 1 and 2). ➋ Evolution keeps the versions of facts that are current at the cutoff. ➌ Composition combines intermediate states layer by layer (Property 3). Each dimension is measured on the gold derivation and its witnesses. The sizes of the support and the witness, the age of the witness, and the vocabulary overlap of the witness with the query measure Access. The number of versions per fact and the number of obsolete events measure Evolution. The height and width of 𝒢q\mathcal{G}_{q} measure Composition. MemDerive samples its workload from CτC_{\tau} while controlling each dimension (Section 3.4). Because each dimension is controlled when queries are generated and measured on every query, a failure can be traced to a specific dimension rather than to the query as a whole.

2.5. Implications for Memory Systems and Evaluation

A memory system can supply derived state in three ways, and the four characteristics confront each way with a different main problem.

Retrieval of records. The system retrieves the records most similar to the query, possibly through a graph or tree index, and leaves the derivation to a language model (Edge et al., 2024; Gutiérrez et al., 2024; Sarthi et al., 2024). Because no record states the derived state (Property 1), the records that support it share few keywords with the query and are semantically distant from it. They are also relevant only together, and their number can exceed any fixed retrieval budget (Property 2). Ranking records by similarity to the query can therefore miss the support for structural reasons, not merely for lack of keywords.

Materialization at ingestion. The system derives and stores states as events arrive (Zhong et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2023). Derived state far outnumbers recorded facts, because intermediate states combine across entities, periods, and categories (Property 3). The system can therefore neither store every derived state nor know in advance which ones will be queried. An event can also invalidate stored states that it never mentions (Property 4), so the system must find those states and re-derive them (Gupta et al., 1993; Motik et al., 2015), and stored state can lag behind the history.

Derivation at query time. The system searches and reasons when a query arrives, as agentic search does (Trivedi et al., 2023). For every query it must gather the full support and combine every layer of intermediate states (Properties 2 and 3), and it recomputes intermediate states that many queries share. Each search and derivation step involves calls to a language model, so answers come with high latency and high token consumption.

Implications for evaluation. Practical systems mix these strategies, and they place the computation in different components with different representations. An evaluation can therefore observe a memory system under test (SUT) only from the outside, through the answers it gives to queries. MemDerive adopts this black-box view and asks three evaluation questions.

  1. Q1.

    Answer reliability (§4.1). Does the SUT answer correctly, with citations to its support? Missed support shows up here first.

  2. Q2.

    Failure diagnosis (§4.2). Where does a wrong answer first depart from the gold derivation, and why? The strategies run into problems at different steps.

  3. Q3.

    Derived-state maintenance (§4.3). Does a correct answer follow the history as it grows, and what does the SUT pay at ingestion and at query time? Stored state can lag, and the strategies place their cost at different stages.

3. Benchmark Construction

MemDerive builds each scenario in three steps, shown in Figure 4. A symbolic specification (Section 3.1) is evaluated into gold (Section 3.2) and then rendered into natural language (Section 3.3). Difficulty control shapes the specification (Section 3.4).

3.1. Scenario Specification

Gold for derived state cannot be annotated reliably by hand, because an answer can depend on many events and on information being absent. MemDerive therefore specifies each scenario symbolically, as events with actions and queries with targets and cutoffs. Natural language enters only at rendering, so the specification alone determines every gold answer.

Scenarios and domains. A scenario is one evolving history together with its rules and queries, and a domain is a family of scenarios that share a workflow. The suite contains 10 scenarios in 3 domains. TripOps covers travel booking and reimbursement, ShopOps covers orders, returns, and spending rules, and EduOps covers degree audits over prerequisite chains. Each scenario adds its own rules, corrections, and cancellations to the workflow of its domain.

Query targets. Query targets are built from operators grouped into five families, and one target can combine several families. Each family exercises a different construct of the derivation program, listed in Table 2. Appendix A lists all operators. Because each construct demands a different computation from an SUT, success on one family says little about another. Table 2 confirms that the families stress different workload dimensions. Each query counts once there, under the family of its main operation. Witness is the mean witness size in events, Obs. the share of queries whose gold derivation excludes an obsolete version, and height and width are means over the gold derivation DAGs.

3.2. Reference Evaluation

The reference evaluator is an executable implementation of the derivation program of Section 2.2. One computation produces the gold answer, the gold derivation DAG, and the witnesses of a query. While computing the answer, the evaluator adds a node to 𝒢q\mathcal{G}_{q} for everything it derives, reads, or checks, together with an edge to each input it uses. Witnesses are extracted from the leaves of 𝒢q\mathcal{G}_{q} and of alternative derivations, and each is checked to be minimal. Because all gold objects come from this one computation, every node of 𝒢q\mathcal{G}_{q} has a known correct state, which Q2 needs, and gold can be recomputed at any cutoff, which Q3 needs.

3.3. Natural-Language Rendering

Rendering produces the record rer_{e} of each event from its actions AeA_{e} and turns each query target into a natural-language question. The specification determines what is correct, and rendering determines how far an SUT must reach from the question to the records that justify the answer.

Faithful records. A record carries every argument of its action, so its fact is recoverable from the text. No record states a derived state, so Property 1 holds by construction.

Entity virtualization. A model that recognizes an entity can answer from pretrained knowledge and skip the records that map the entity to a category. Rendering therefore invents every recognizable entity, including people, organizations, places, products, courses, and currencies, so that every mapping must come from the history.

Access in rendering. Questions use the vocabulary of derived predicates, and they often refer to an entity through an associated event, a date, or a place rather than its identifier. For some queries, the key terms of the question appear in distractor records, which leave the answer unchanged, but in none of the supporting records.

3.4. Difficulty Control

When generating a scenario, the generator sets how demanding each query is in each workload dimension (Erling et al., 2015). Queries therefore spread over a range of difficulty in every dimension, and the dimension measures of Section 2.4 record where each query falls.

Access. Support is harder to gather when its events are far apart and do not resemble the question. Through dispersion, the generator spreads the events of one witness over the history, and rendering adds the lexical gaps, indirect references, and distractors of Section 3.3.

Evolution. Current versions are harder to identify when facts are revised often and obsolete records appear late. The generator builds update chains that revise a fact several times and places obsolete records late in the history.

Composition. A query is harder to compose when it combines more kinds of reasoning. The generator varies this number, the composition degree, from a single operation to combinations of version resolution, rule application, and checking that a collection is complete.

Quota bands. Target shares of operator families, witness sizes, and answer types keep the workload off the easiest cases.

3.5. Suite Statistics

Table 3 summarizes the ten scenarios. Because scenarios are generated from configurations, new scenarios of the same design can be generated whenever existing ones may have entered the training data of a model.

4. Evaluation Methodology

The protocol follows the black-box view of Section 2.5. For every query, an SUT returns a context, the text it supplies for answering, and one answer model shared by all SUTs turns it into an answer, an answerability label, and cited events. Every measurement below is obtained by posing questions to the SUT.

4.1. Q1: Answer Reliability

Q1 asks whether an SUT answers correctly and cites its support. A correct answer alone is weak evidence, because Booleans and empty sets can be guessed and a total can be right by coincidence.

Answer scoring. Answers are scored deterministically. Every gold answer has a type, and each type has its own equivalence test for numbers, Booleans, collections, or accepted aliases. No language model is therefore needed to judge an answer, and scores are fully reproducible. Answer accuracy (𝖠𝗇𝗌𝖠𝖼𝖼\mathsf{AnsAcc}) requires the returned answer to match yqy_{q} for an 𝖺𝗇𝗌𝗐𝖾𝗋𝖺𝖻𝗅𝖾\mathsf{answerable} or 𝗃𝗎𝗌𝗍𝗂𝖿𝗂𝖾𝖽​-​𝗓𝖾𝗋𝗈\mathsf{justified\text{-}zero} query and the 𝗎𝗇𝗄𝗇𝗈𝗐𝗇\mathsf{unknown} label otherwise. Answerability accuracy (𝖠𝗇𝗌𝖻𝗅𝖠𝖼𝖼\mathsf{AnsblAcc}) scores the label alone.

Citation scoring. MemDerive also scores the cited events E^q\hat{E}_{q} against the support and witnesses of Section 2.3:

(2) pE​(q)=|E^q∩S⁡(q)||E^q|,rW​(q)=maxW∈𝒲⁡(q)⁡|E^q∩W||W|.p_{E}(q)=\frac{|\hat{E}_{q}\cap S(q)|}{|\hat{E}_{q}|},\qquad r_{W}(q)=\max_{W\in\mathcal{W}(q)}\frac{|\hat{E}_{q}\cap W|}{|W|}.

Their harmonic mean is the citation F1F_{1}. Witnessed accuracy (𝖶𝗂𝗍𝖠𝖼𝖼\mathsf{WitAcc}) counts a query as correct when its answer is correct and both pEp_{E} and rWr_{W} reach 0.50.5. A correct answer then counts only if most of its citations are relevant and cover a substantial part of one witness, without requiring a complete citation list. The two scores encode two design decisions. Precision checks citations against the whole support S⁡(q)S(q), so citing additional supporting events costs nothing. Recall takes the best match over all witnesses, so an SUT that follows a different valid derivation loses nothing. The shares of queries that cite an obsolete event or a distractor complement both scores.

4.2. Q2: Failure Diagnosis

Q2 asks where a wrong answer arises and why. Because SUTs are black boxes, diagnosis cannot inspect their internal state. It can only ask further questions, and 𝒢q\mathcal{G}_{q} tells it which questions to ask and what their correct answers are.

4.2.1. Failure Classes

A wrong answer arises at some state of the derivation. The SUT may be able to produce that state but fail to gather it when the derivation needs it, or it may fail to produce the state even when asked for it directly. Each case calls for a different repair, so MemDerive distinguishes three failure classes.

  • •

    A state is ungathered when the SUT returns it when asked for it directly, but the request for the state that needs it does not gather it.

  • •

    A resolved fact or rule is unretrievable when the SUT cannot return it even when asked for it directly.

  • •

    A derived state is misderived when the SUT derives it wrongly even when asked for it directly, although its inputs are gathered.

The classes follow the workload dimensions of Section 2.4. Ungathered states are failures of Access. Unretrievable facts arise at Access or Evolution, depending on whether the fact has a superseded version, and misderived states arise at Composition.

4.2.2. State Probes

Any node of 𝒢q\mathcal{G}_{q} that holds a resolved fact, a rule, or a derived state can be asked about directly.

Definition 0 (State probe).

A state probe of a node vv in 𝒢q\mathcal{G}_{q} is a natural-language question at the cutoff of qq whose gold answer is the state of vv.

Probes are rendered from fixed templates, and their gold answers come from the reference evaluator, so no language model writes or grades them. The suite contains 2,818 probes for 1,029 queries. The probed nodes, connected by the dependencies of 𝒢q\mathcal{G}_{q}, form the diagnostic DAG 𝒟q\mathcal{D}_{q}. Every SUT answers the same probes for the same queries in the same order.

Two contexts. Each probe is answered under two contexts. In the inherited context, the answer model receives the context that the SUT returned for the question of a parent node, which for the children of the root rqr_{q} is the original query. This reproduces what the derivation had available when it needed the state. For the root, the inherited answer is the original answer. In the targeted context, the probe itself is sent to the SUT as a new query, and the answer model receives the context returned for it. This tests whether the SUT can return the information when asked for it directly. Let ts​(v)∈{0,1}t_{s}(v)\in\{0,1\} indicate whether SUT ss answers the probe of vv correctly in the targeted context. Because a node can have several parents, inherited correctness belongs to an edge. For a child uu of vv, is​(u∣v)∈{0,1}i_{s}(u\mid v)\in\{0,1\} indicates whether ss answers the probe of uu correctly in the context returned for the question of vv, and is​(rq)i_{s}(r_{q}) indicates whether the original answer is correct.

4.2.3. Failure Localization

A wrong probe answer does not by itself locate a failure, because an error can propagate upward, and a node computed correctly from a wrong input is wrong as well. The failure arises at a node that is wrong although all of its inputs are right. Such nodes mark where an SUT first departs from the gold derivation, and together they form its failure frontier. Localization uses the inherited context, because it shows whether each request gathered the states it needed.

Definition 0 (Failure frontier).

A probed node vv lies on the failure frontier of SUT ss when some path rq=v0,…,vk=vr_{q}=v_{0},\dots,v_{k}=v in 𝒟q\mathcal{D}_{q} has is​(rq)=0i_{s}(r_{q})=0 and is​(vj∣vj−1)=0i_{s}(v_{j}\mid v_{j-1})=0 for every jj, and is​(u∣v)=1i_{s}(u\mid v)=1 for every child uu of vv.

A derivation can have one frontier node per failing branch. The targeted context determines the class of a frontier node vv. If ts​(v)=1t_{s}(v)=1, the SUT returns vv when asked directly, so vv is ungathered. Otherwise vv is unretrievable if it is a resolved fact or rule, and misderived if it is a derived state, because the inputs of vv were gathered. Algorithm 1 locates the frontier and classifies each of its nodes. It uses only probe answers, so diagnosis needs no access to the internals of the SUT.

4.2.4. Interventions

A frontier shows that a state is wrong while the answer is wrong, which is a co-occurrence rather than an explanation. Two recoveries test whether the departure matters for the answer. Both rebuild the answer bottom-up along 𝒟q\mathcal{D}_{q}. Each branch is followed down to a node that the SUT answers correctly in the targeted context, or to a leaf, and the answer model recomputes every node above these stopping nodes from its children. The two recoveries differ only in the states at the stopping nodes. Figure 5 marks their results with ➊ and ➋.

➊ Self-evidence recovery. The stopping nodes keep the SUT’s targeted answers, so every state comes from the SUT. Success shows that the SUT can return the evidence the answer needs and that the original failure lay in gathering and combining it.

➋ Gold-evidence recovery. Wrong stopping nodes, which are leaves, take their gold states instead, and everything else stays as the SUT produced it. Success where self-evidence recovery fails shows that the wrong evidence causes the failure. We call such evidence load-bearing.

Discussion. The two recoveries complement the failure classes. Self-evidence recovery can repair an ungathered failure, because the SUT returns the state when asked directly. Gold-evidence recovery can also repair an unretrievable one. A failure that persists after gold-evidence recovery lies above the evidence, in how states are combined. Both recoveries measure how much of a failure can be recovered with assistance.

Example 0 (Diagnosis of Example 2.3).

An SUT answers three instead of two. In Figure 5, node colors show its probe answers in the inherited context. Vera’s home country, the set of trips, and the countries of Trip-Anser and Trip-Ibex are right, but Trip-Grus is placed in Drossel. Both inputs of that state are wrong, so both lie on the frontier. The destination of Trip-Grus is Halewick from the obsolete e7e_{7}, also in the targeted context, so this resolved fact is unretrievable, and its dimension is Evolution. The country of Corby is missing from the context of its parent, but the targeted context returns Corvia, so this fact is ungathered. The tags beside the failing nodes show what each recovery computes from the stopping nodes upward. Self-evidence recovery repairs the ungathered fact, but Halewick contradicts it, so the country of Trip-Grus stays unknown and the count is still wrong. Gold-evidence recovery replaces Halewick with Corby and yields two, so the obsolete destination is load-bearing.

4.3. Q3: Derived-State Maintenance

Q3 asks whether an SUT keeps derived state correct as the history grows. By Property 4, an answer that is correct at one cutoff need not remain correct at the next, and an SUT that materializes state may lag behind the history. One snapshot cannot measure maintenance.

Fixed-query trajectories. The evaluation fixes a sequence of cutoffs τ1<⋯<τm\tau_{1}<\cdots<\tau_{m}, called checkpoints, spread over the history. A tracked query fixes its target θ\theta and is asked at every checkpoint, and qj=(θ,τj)q_{j}=(\theta,\tau_{j}) denotes its instance at checkpoint jj. The reference evaluator recomputes gold at each checkpoint, which yields the trajectory z⁡(q1),…,z⁡(qm)z(q_{1}),\ldots,z(q_{m}). Before each checkpoint, the SUT ingests the new events into its existing memory, so it must update that memory rather than rebuild it.

Refresh and preservation. Consecutive checkpoints j−1j-1 and jj form a transition. Let dj(q)=𝟏[z(qj)≠z(qj−1)]d_{j}(q)=\mathbf{1}[z(q_{j})\neq z(q_{j-1})], and call the transition changed when dj​(q)=1d_{j}(q)=1 and unchanged otherwise. Tracked queries are sampled so that both kinds of transition occur often. Refresh measures whether a change reaches the answer, and preservation measures whether an unaffected answer survives. With cs,j​(q)c_{s,j}(q) indicating that SUT ss answers qjq_{j} correctly,

(3) Refreshs\displaystyle\operatorname{Refresh}_{s} =∑q,jdj​(q)​cs,j−1​(q)​cs,j​(q)∑q,jdj​(q)​cs,j−1​(q),\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{q,j}d_{j}(q)\,c_{s,j-1}(q)\,c_{s,j}(q)}{\sum_{q,j}d_{j}(q)\,c_{s,j-1}(q)},
Preservations\displaystyle\operatorname{Preservation}_{s} =∑q,j(1−dj​(q))​cs,j−1​(q)​cs,j​(q)∑q,j(1−dj​(q))​cs,j−1​(q).\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{q,j}(1-d_{j}(q))\,c_{s,j-1}(q)\,c_{s,j}(q)}{\sum_{q,j}(1-d_{j}(q))\,c_{s,j-1}(q)}.

Both rates condition on a correct previous answer. The condition separates maintenance from initial difficulty, since an SUT that never answered correctly has nothing to maintain.

Definition 0 (Explicit and implicit change).

A changed transition at checkpoint jj is explicit if some event ee with τj−1<te≤τj\tau_{j-1}<t_{e}\leq\tau_{j} belongs to a witness of qjq_{j} and an action in AeA_{e} asserts a fact that contains the new answer. Otherwise the change is implicit.

An implicit change is the case that Property 4 describes, because no arriving record mentions the state that changed. Comparing refresh across the two kinds shows whether an SUT propagates a change through dependencies or only updates what it is told. The latter is the lag that Section 2.5 attributes to materialization. In Example 2.3, e10e_{10} makes an implicit change: it books a hotel, yet the count drops from three to two.

Complementary measures. Four further measures complement the two rates.

  • •

    Stale-answer rate. The share of changed transitions at which the SUT still returns the previous gold answer. It distinguishes a missed update from a wrong one.

  • •

    Recovery delay. The number of checkpoints from a changed transition until the SUT first answers correctly.

  • •

    Continuous correctness. The share of tracked queries answered correctly at every checkpoint up to τj\tau_{j}. It combines initial difficulty with maintenance.

  • •

    Ingestion and query-time cost. The cost of ingesting events and of answering queries, recorded separately. It shows where each SUT places its work among the strategies of Section 2.5.

5. Experiments

5.1. Experimental Setup

SUTs and reference conditions. The SUTs are four memory systems and two raw-retrieval baselines. The memory systems are Mem0 (Chhikara et al., 2025), Cognee (Markovic et al., 2025), LightMem (Fang et al., 2026), and MemoryOS (Kang et al., 2025). They cover extracted-fact stores, graph-oriented memory, and hierarchical organizations. The baselines rank the history with BM25 or with dense embeddings (Embed) and return the top items. They retrieve session documents by default, and figures mark session-level and event-level variants as -S and -E where both appear. Three reference conditions bound the results. Closed-Book receives no history, Full-Context receives the whole visible history, and Oracle receives the support S⁡(q)S(q), all events that contribute to the answer.

Models and defaults. The answer model is GPT-5.6 Sol with reasoning disabled and temperature zero. All SUTs share our answer and judge prompts, released with the artifact. The judge prompt is stricter than those used in the original benchmarks, so scores can differ from previously reported ones. Memory systems that extract memories at ingestion use GPT-5.6 Luna as the extraction model. Dense retrieval uses Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B (Zhang et al., 2025). Every SUT returns k=15k=15 items per query. Mem0 and LightMem do not return event identifiers, so their citations are mapped to events through the recorded memory attribution.

Query sets. The main comparison asks all 1,503 queries of the 10 scenarios at the end of each history, over 4,692 events. The context-budget comparison caps the context at 500 to 16K tokens on 400 queries. Diagnosis probes the complete diagnostic DAGs of a subset of queries from every scenario, the diagnostic queries. Maintenance tracks 132 queries at five checkpoints, at 20%, 40%, 60%, 80%, and 100% of each history. Transition analysis uses the tracked queries whose gold is never 𝗎𝗇𝗄𝗇𝗈𝗐𝗇\mathsf{unknown}, which contain 106 changed transitions. For comparison, the SUTs are also evaluated on LoCoMo and LongMemEval (Maharana et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025) with their official question sets. The artifact also records model settings, per-query outputs, and the inputs of every figure.

5.2. Q1: Answer Reliability

Memory systems trail raw retrieval. Figure 6 reports the main comparison. The four memory systems reach 30.41–48.30% answer accuracy, and even the strongest, Mem0, trails BM25 at 58.28%. Full-Context and Oracle reach 79.84% and 96.01% under the same answer model, so the gap lies in what the SUTs supply. Witnessed accuracy, answerability accuracy, and citation precision, recall, and F1F_{1} show the same order.

The gap persists under matched context budgets. Figure 7 caps the context of every SUT at the same number of tokens. Mem0 plateaus at 77.25% from 8K tokens, and at 16K event-level BM25 still leads with 78.75%. A larger budget therefore does not favor memory over raw retrieval. With the whole history, medium reasoning raises accuracy from 80.00% to 93.25%, so reasoning also matters once all evidence is present. Oracle needs only 712 tokens on average.

Accuracy falls along every workload dimension. Figures 8 and 9 split the main comparison by the measures of Section 2.4. For Access, memory systems fall from 73.19–93.48% when the support holds one event to 14.77–26.85% when it holds ten or more, and Mem0 falls from 83.42% to 25.82% from the nearest to the farthest quartile of witness age. For Evolution, 20.33% of Mem0’s answers in that farthest quartile cite an obsolete event. For Composition, accuracy falls with the composition degree and, even among shallow derivations, with width, for Mem0 from 83.05% to 21.97%. On high and wide derivations, Oracle still reaches 86.80%, whereas memory systems reach 15.25–25.22%, so width matters alongside height. Across operator families (Figure 10), set and quantitative queries are the hardest.

Rankings on existing benchmarks do not carry over. Figure 11 compares the same conditions on LoCoMo, LongMemEval, and MemDerive. On LongMemEval, Mem0 reaches 84.00% and exceeds BM25 at 78.60%. On LoCoMo, Cognee reaches 68.13%, close to BM25 at 70.64%. On MemDerive, BM25 exceeds all four memory systems. Each benchmark keeps its own question set, so the comparison holds within each panel.

5.3. Q2: Failure Diagnosis

Diagnosis runs Algorithm 1 on the complete diagnostic DAGs for the raw-retrieval baselines and the four memory systems. Table 4 reports the targeted accuracy, the share of state probes that an SUT answers correctly in the targeted context, for four kinds of node. They are resolved facts, rules, completeness facts, which assert that a collection is complete, and derived states. The table also reports the failure classes and both recoveries as shares of wrong answers. A wrong answer can contain frontier nodes of several classes.

Rules and derived states are hard to return. The targeted columns of Table 4 show what each SUT can return when asked directly. Facts and completeness facts are mostly returned. Rules are not. Mem0 answers 17% of rule probes and LightMem 8%, so their derivations lose the rules they apply. Derived states are returned for only 26–61% of probes, and LightMem returns only 56% of facts.

Most failures are ungathered. Every wrong answer has at least one frontier node. For memory systems, 61–85% of wrong answers contain an ungathered state, which the SUT returns when asked for it directly but which the request for the state that needs it does not gather. LightMem differs, as 83% of its wrong answers contain an unretrievable fact, which it cannot return even when asked directly. Misderived states occur most often for BM25, which gathers its evidence most completely.

Requests for derived states miss their inputs. Figure 12(a) compares the targeted and inherited contexts on every edge of 𝒟q\mathcal{D}_{q}, by how many levels the child lies above the deepest level of 𝒟q\mathcal{D}_{q}. The shaded distance holds a single query. The two contexts agree on the deepest level, which holds facts read from events. One level above, they separate. The targeted context answers 86–94% of these states for BM25, Cognee, and Mem0, whereas the inherited context answers only 54–74%. Each input can be retrieved alone, but the request for the derived state does not bring all of them together, as Property 2 predicts.

The recoveries confirm the classes. Self-evidence recovery raises accuracy by up to 30.0 points (Figure 12(b)). It repairs 33–52% of the wrong answers of Mem0, Cognee, and MemoryOS, whose failures are mostly ungathered, but only 9% for LightMem. Gold-evidence recovery repairs 39–65% of memory-system failures and adds 39 points for LightMem, so its wrong evidence is load-bearing. The failures that remain lie in how states are combined.

An early correct state does not ensure recovery. Figure 12(c) relates how close to the root the first correct state of a failed query lies to the accuracy after self-evidence recovery. BM25 finds its first correct state 1.38 levels below the root on average and recovers to 80.00%, whereas LightMem finds it 2.52 levels below and recovers to 47.50%. An SUT whose correct states lie closer to the root leaves fewer levels to rebuild. Recovery still needs correct states on every branch, so one correct state is not enough.

5.4. Q3: Derived-State Maintenance

Refresh lags preservation. Figure 13(a) reports both rates of Equation 3. Memory systems preserve 91.03–92.86% of unaffected answers but refresh only 35.71–63.64% of changed ones. LightMem refreshes least and Mem0 most.

Implicit changes are refreshed least. Of the 106 changed transitions, 18 are explicit and 88 are implicit. Memory systems refresh 82.4% of explicit changes but only 41.1% of implicit ones (Table 5). Raw retrieval refreshes 83.3% and 63.1%. Memory systems thus update what a new record states but rarely propagate a change through dependencies, which is the lag that Section 2.5 attributes to materialization. Raw retrieval derives at query time and loses less. Stale answers point the same way. Memory systems repeat the previous answer mostly after implicit changes, whereas raw retrieval goes stale mostly after explicit ones, because the superseded record still matches the query.

Missed updates persist. Figure 13(b) adds the regression and stale-answer rates. Memory systems repeat the previous gold answer in 9.43–18.87% of changed transitions. Recovery delay shows that, by the last checkpoint, 66–79 of the 106 changes remain unrecovered for memory systems, against 1 for Oracle.

Few answers stay correct throughout. Figure 14 reports continuous correctness. Memory systems fall from 28.03–65.15% at the first checkpoint to 16.67–41.67% at the last, raw retrieval ends near 43.18%, and Oracle keeps 93.18%.

5.5. Ingestion and Query-Time Cost

Memory systems shift cost to ingestion. Figure 15 follows the ingestion checkpoints. Memory systems pay for model calls at ingestion, up to $2.60 for MemoryOS, whereas BM25 and Embed make none. Their median retrieval latency reaches seconds for Cognee and MemoryOS, against 8.1 ms for BM25.

Ingestion work does not buy reliability. Over all queries (Figure 16), memory systems spend $0.31–2.57 at ingestion and $9.13–37.67 on answering, against $73.55 for answering with BM25, because they pass the answer model less text. This saving is real, but the work done at ingestion neither closes the accuracy gap of Q1 nor refreshes implicit changes. Which placement pays off depends on how often the history changes and how often its states are reused.

6. Discussion

6.1. Lessons for Memory Systems

Read together, the results of Q1 to Q3 and the cost measurements yield five lessons for the design of memory systems.

L1: The bottleneck is gathering, not storage. Asked directly, BM25, Cognee, and Mem0 return 86–94 % of the states one level above the evidence, but only 54–74 % within the context of the request that needs them, and most failures are ungathered. A memory should therefore split a request for a derived state along its derivation into requests for its inputs. Self-evidence recovery, which does exactly this, raises accuracy by up to 30.0 points.

L2: Rules must be stored as first-class objects. Asked directly, Mem0 returns 17 % of rules and LightMem 8 %. Fact-centric extraction summarizes policies and exceptions away, although every derived state applies them. Rules should be stored with their versions, like facts.

L3: Once gathering works, composition becomes the bottleneck. BM25 gathers evidence most completely, yet 38 % of its wrong answers contain a misderived state, and accuracy falls with derivation width and on set and aggregate queries. Better retrieval alone therefore has diminishing returns. Sets, aggregates, and completeness checks call for explicit operators, and completeness must be recorded so that a system can tell an empty answer from an unknown one.

L4: Materialization without dependency tracking makes state stale. Memory systems refresh 82.4 % of explicit changes but 41.1 % of implicit ones, whereas raw retrieval refreshes 83.3 % and 63.1 %. Their stale answers also arise on opposite kinds of change. A memory system must track what each stored state depends on and recompute it when an input changes, as incremental view maintenance does (Gupta et al., 1993; Motik et al., 2015). Raw retrieval instead needs version resolution to suppress superseded records.

L5: Ingestion should build structure, not summaries. Memory systems pay at ingestion and pass the answer model less text, yet they trail raw retrieval in accuracy and in refresh. Work at ingestion pays off only when it records what derivations consume, namely versions, rules, dependencies, and completeness.

6.2. Scope

Executable scenarios make every answer and its derivation checkable. They cover version resolution, rules, dependencies, sets, aggregation, and completeness, but not subjective preferences or open-ended planning. The shared answer model isolates what each SUT supplies, and the recoveries use the decomposition that the benchmark provides.

7. Related Work

Agent memory systems. Memory systems differ in how they organize a history (Wu et al., 2026b). MemGPT (Packer et al., 2023) manages a hierarchy of memory resources, Mem0 (Chhikara et al., 2025) extracts and updates salient facts, MemoryLLM (Wang et al., 2024a) keeps memory in model parameters, MemoryOS (Kang et al., 2025) and LightMem (Fang et al., 2026) stage memory across levels, and Cognee (Markovic et al., 2025), Zep (Rasmussen et al., 2025), and AriGraph (Anokhin et al., 2025) link stored information in graphs. StateMemBench (Fan et al., 2026) and STALE (Chao et al., 2026) make supersession, dependencies, and invalidation explicit. MemDerive prescribes none of these representations. It evaluates their observable effect, whether the requested state is correct, whether its inputs can be recovered, and whether later changes reach it.

Memory benchmarks. LoCoMo (Maharana et al., 2024), LoCoMo-Plus (Li et al., 2026b), and LongMemEval (Wu et al., 2025) test recall, temporal and multi-session reasoning, knowledge updates, and abstention over long conversations, and MemoryAgentBench (Hu et al., 2026) adds incremental evaluation of retrieval, learning, and forgetting. MemBench (Tan et al., 2025), MEMTRACK (Deshpande et al., 2025), LongMemEval-V2 (Wu et al., 2026a), MemoryArena (He et al., 2026), AMemGym (Jiayang et al., 2026), and AMA-Bench (Zhao et al., 2026) move these tests into agentic tasks. Recent benchmarks target specific failures. StateMemBench (Fan et al., 2026) separates current from superseded answers, MemTrace (Long et al., 2026) audits how evidence is reached and used, StreamMemBench (Liu et al., 2026) follows the reuse of feedback, InMind (Li et al., 2026a) separates missing facts from facts that are stored but not surfaced, and Ground Truth First (Spencer, 2026) checks memory against a script generated before the text. Table 6 compares their evaluations. Answers are scored by exact comparison, by a model judge, or by a mix of both. Evidence names what is checked besides the answer, namely retrieved sources, stored facts, or cited events against witnesses. The tests mark whether a benchmark evaluates revised versions of facts, maintenance of answers as the history grows, and probes of intermediate derived states. MemDerive adds a reference derivation for every query, which makes intermediate states testable and is recomputed at every checkpoint.

Provenance and view maintenance. Database provenance explains how query results, including aggregates, depend on input records (Green et al., 2007; Amsterdamer et al., 2011), and why and why-not provenance explain returned and missing results (Buneman et al., 2001; Lee et al., 2019). Incremental view maintenance updates derived results when base data changes (Gupta et al., 1993; Motik et al., 2015), including higher-order delta processing and stream computation (Koch et al., 2014; Budiu et al., 2023). MemDerive builds its witnesses on minimal why-provenance and recomputes gold as the history grows. It applies these ideas to memory over natural-language records, where the SUT must first recover the facts that a database would be given.

8. Conclusion

Agent memory must supply derived state, which no record states and which changes as the history evolves. MemDerive makes this requirement measurable. Symbolic scenarios give every query an exact answer, a gold derivation DAG, and its supporting events, so the benchmark can check final answers, locate the intermediate state where a derivation fails, and follow answers across updates. Our evaluation shows that current memory systems trail raw retrieval on derived state, that most of their failures are intermediate states they can return but do not retrieve for the question that needs them, and that they rarely propagate implicit changes. Reliable agent memory therefore needs dependency-aware gathering, versioned rules, and incremental maintenance of derived state, much as a database maintains views over changing tables.
